extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics studying methods of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on novelist's method: choice and management of point of view, treatment (pictorial vs dramatic), handling of setting and secondary characters, and how to deploy variety of method without loss of unity. Uses close readings of Madame Bovary and Vanity Fair as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steady direction of stages and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Each stage of the story is steadily directed. By the time the scene is reached, nothing is wanting to its opportunity; the action is ripe, the place resonant; and then the incident takes up the story, conclusively establishes one aspect of it and opens the view towards the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange episodes so each stage prepares the next: scenes should feel 'ripe' and resonant, and summaries should carry the reader forward toward the next climax. Avoid leaving scenes undeveloped or disjointed; ensure rapid summaries and pauses are used to maintain momentum towards the larger climactic points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide the centre of vision (point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficult question of the centre of vision. With which of the characters, if with any of them, is the writer to identify himself, which is he to 'go behind'? Which of these vessels of thought and feeling is he to reveal from within?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine early which mind will principally 'command the subject.' If the subject can be completely rendered by showing it through a single figure, do not range further. Unnecessary plunges into other characters' inner lives confuse the effect; shift point of view no more often than necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial objectivity vs interior access
rubrics_metrics.description: I suppose his unwritten story to rise before him, its main lines settled, as something at first entirely objective, the whole thing seen from without — the linked chain of incident, the men and women in their places. ... Such restraint is burdensome, unless in a very compact and straightforward tale. Somewhere the author must break into the privacy of his characters and open their minds to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether the narrative will remain mainly external/objective or will enter characters' consciousness. Use restraint if staying outside; where inner life must be shown, do so deliberately and sparingly, balancing the need for interior revelation with the risks of breaking the narrative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid haphazard plunges into inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Haphazard and unnecessary plunges into the inner life of the characters only confuse the effect, changing the focus without compensating gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only enter a character's mind when it meaningfully advances understanding of the subject. Random or gratuitous shifts in subjective perspective dilute focus and can alienate readers; every subjective access should have a clear purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the true subject (character alone vs character-in-environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true subject of the novel is not given by a mere summary of the course which is taken by the story. She may be there for her own sake, simply, or for the sake of the predicament in which she stands... perhaps, on the other hand, she is a hapless sufferer in the clash between her aspirations and her fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your work is essentially a portrait (the character for their own sake) or a study of a character within and against a setting (drama/conflict). This decision dictates choices of setting, secondary characters, and whether the environment must be treated as integral or merely background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial treatment vs dramatic emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: He makes it perfectly clear that his view is not centred upon the actual outcome of Emma's predicament... He makes nothing of the suspense or dramatic value; events are only Flaubert's way of telling his subject, of making it count to the eye. They are not in themselves what he has to say, they simply illustrate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether interest will rest on the pictorial impression (rendering lives, impressions, and character) or on dramatic plotting and decisive incidents. If pictorial, focus on vivid, characteristic scenes and atmosphere rather than on precipitate climaxes; if dramatic, structure events to build toward decisive turning points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat setting and minor types as integral
rubrics_metrics.description: The town with its life is not behind his heroine, subdued in tone to make a background; it is with her, no less fully to the front; its value in the picture is as strong as her own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject requires it, render scenery and 'indigenous gossips' with as much distinctness as principal characters. Settings and secondary figures may be essential to the book's subject and must be characterized with care rather than left as mere backdrop.

rubrics_metrics.name: When protagonist's perception is limited, supply extra vision
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is the experience and the actual taste of it that is to be imparted, the story must be viewed as the poor creature saw it; and yet the poor creature cannot tell the story in full. A shift of the vision is necessary. The author's wit, therefore, and none other, must supply what is wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your central viewpoint character lacks perception or wit to render the world fully, plan how the narrator/authorial perspective will supply missing information. Do so without jolting the reader out of immersion—transitions must be smooth and discreet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make transitions between subjective and authorial vision unobtrusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition must be made without awkwardness, without calling attention to it. ... There is nothing more disconcerting in a novel than to see the writer changing his part in this way — throwing off the character into which he has been projecting himself and taking a new stand outside and away from the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blatant, clumsy shifts from a character's consciousness to an overt authorial voice. Use tonal cues, subtle irony, and measured distance so the reader does not feel 'wrenched' out of shared experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a measured distance / ironic aloofness
rubrics_metrics.description: He deals with the difficulty ... by keeping Emma always at a certain distance, even when he appears to be entering her mind most freely. He makes her subjective ... but he does so with an air of aloofness that forbids us ever to become entirely identified with her. A hint of irony is always perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If employing a subjective portrayal of a limited or foolish character, consider preserving a subtle authorial aloofness (irony) so readers can observe the character without being wholly immersed. Use tone to imply judgment rather than blunt authorial statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal valuation in tone rather than in explicit comment
rubrics_metrics.description: He knows it without asserting it, needless to say; his valuation of her is only implied; it is in his tone — never in his words, which invariably respect her own estimate of herself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the narrator's assessment be implicit in diction, ironic contrasts, and the structuring of scenes instead of explicit authorial condemnation. This preserves realism and reader trust while still guiding interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt authorial intrusion or boastful independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps it is only Thackeray, among the great, who seems to find a positively wilful pleasure in damaging his own story by open maltreatment of this kind; there are times when Thackeray will even boast of his own independence, insisting in so many words on his freedom to say what he pleases about his men and women and to make them behave as he will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not relish or display open intrusions that damage dramatic immersion. Authorial asides that 'boast' independence can weaken the story; privilege subtlety and craft over self-congratulatory commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare alternative viewpoints for later effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Charles must be held in readiness, so to speak, for these last pages; his inner mind, and his point of view, must be created in advance and kept in reserve, so that the force of the climax, when it is reached, may be instantly felt. And so we have the early episodes of Charles's youth ... and Flaubert's questionable manner of working round to his subject is explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a later revelation or climax depends on another character's perspective, plant that perspective earlier in the narrative so the payoff feels earned. Early episodes and background for secondary characters are legitimate preparatory elements, not mere digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use variety of method sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that with its variety of method, and with its careful restriction of that variety to its bare needs, and with its scrupulous use of its resources — it is a book, altogether, that gives a good point of departure for an examination of the methods of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix techniques (panoramic vs scenic, pictorial vs dramatic, objective vs subjective) only as required by the subject. Reserve variety to what the material asks for; unnecessary complexity dissipates impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between panoramic and scenic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between the 'panoramic' and the 'scenic' presentation of a story... Thackeray saw them as broad expanses, stretches of territory, to be surveyed from edge to edge with a sweeping glance... The landscape lay before him, his imagination wandered freely across it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide if the narrative aims to survey a wide social landscape (panoramic) or to focus on closely staged scenes (scenic). For a panoramic novel, unity may rest on typifying a world or society rather than on tightly interwoven plotlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure unity through typifying impression rather than plot alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Not in any complication of incident, therefore, nor in any single strife of will, is the subject of Vanity Fair to be discerned. It is in the impression of a world, a society, a time — certain manners of life ... The book is not the story of any of them, it is the story which they unite to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work is a panorama, aim for unity by ensuring characters and episodes collectively produce a consistent, typical impression of the setting or theme rather than relying solely on an intricate plot to bind the book together.
